questions.topic: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.question: Who were Australia’s first inhabitants?
options: Convicts who arrived on the First Fleet
The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
Free settlers from Great Britain and Ireland
questions.explanation: The booklet says Australia’s first inhabitants are the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
questions.source: Part 1 › Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples › p. 8

questions.topic: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.question: What does the booklet say about the cultures and traditions of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples?
options: They began when the colonies united in 1901
They are the oldest continuous cultures and traditions in the world
They started during the gold rush of the 1850s
questions.explanation: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have the oldest continuous cultures and traditions in the world.
questions.source: Part 1 › Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples › p. 8

questions.topic: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.question: Historically, where are Aboriginal people from?
options: Islands between Queensland and Papua New Guinea
questions.explanation: Historically, Aboriginal people are from mainland Australia and Tasmania. Torres Strait Islander people are from the islands between the northern tip of Queensland and Papua New Guinea.
questions.source: Part 1 › Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples › p. 8

questions.topic: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.question: Where are Torres Strait Islander people from?
options: The island of Tasmania, across the Bass Strait
The desert regions in the east of Western Australia
Islands between the northern tip of Queensland and Papua New Guinea
questions.explanation: Torres Strait Islander people are from the islands between the northern tip of Queensland and Papua New Guinea.
questions.source: Part 1 › Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples › p. 8

questions.topic: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.question: Approximately how long have Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples been in Australia?
options: Since the First Fleet arrived in 1788
questions.explanation: The booklet says Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have been here for approximately 65,000 years. The archaeological record puts the arrival of Aboriginal peoples between 65,000 and 40,000 years ago.
questions.source: Part 1 › Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples › p. 8

questions.topic: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.question: According to the booklet, when do the creation stories of Aboriginal peoples begin?
options: With the arrival of the First Fleet
With the federation of Australia in 1901
questions.explanation: Aboriginal peoples believe they are central to the creation stories of this land, and their creation stories commence with the beginning of time.
questions.source: Part 1 › Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples › p. 8

questions.topic: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.question: How is the deep connection of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples with the land expressed?
options: In the laws of the first colony
In their stories, art and dance
In the colours of the national flag
questions.explanation: They have a deep connection with the land, which is expressed in their stories, art and dance.
questions.source: Part 1 › Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples › p. 8

questions.topic: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.question: Which statement about Indigenous cultures is correct?
options: They are all the same and are not part of Australia’s national identity
They are diverse and an important part of Australia’s national identity
They stopped being practised when European settlement started
questions.explanation: The booklet says Indigenous cultures are diverse and an important part of Australia’s national identity.
questions.source: Part 1 › Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples › p. 8

questions.topic: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.question: Which statement about the age-old beliefs and traditions of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples is correct?
options: They stopped being followed when the colonies were formed
They still guide Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples today
They were replaced by British traditions at Federation in 1901
questions.explanation: The booklet says Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have age-old beliefs and traditions that still guide them today.
questions.source: Part 1 › Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples › p. 8

questions.topic: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.question: In the booklet, what does the word ‘Indigenous’ refer to?
options: People who arrived in Australia with the First Fleet
Migrants who came to Australia after World War II
The Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander peoples of Australia
questions.explanation: The glossary defines ‘Indigenous’ as the Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander peoples of Australia.
questions.source: Glossary › Indigenous › p. 42

questions.topic: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.question: Which group of people is historically from mainland Australia and Tasmania?
options: The convicts of the First Fleet
questions.explanation: Historically, Aboriginal people are from mainland Australia and Tasmania.
questions.source: Part 1 › Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples › p. 8

questions.question: When did the First Fleet arrive from Great Britain?
questions.explanation: European settlement started when the First Fleet arrived from Great Britain on 26 January 1788.
questions.source: Part 1 › Early days of European settlement › p. 8

questions.question: How many convict ships made up the First Fleet?
questions.explanation: European settlement started when the first 11 convict ships, which became known as the ‘First Fleet’, arrived from Great Britain.
questions.source: Part 1 › Early days of European settlement › p. 8

questions.question: Where did the First Fleet come from?
questions.explanation: The First Fleet arrived from Great Britain on 26 January 1788.
questions.source: Part 1 › Early days of European settlement › p. 8

questions.question: Why did the British Government decide to send convicts to Australia?
options: The British Government wanted convicts to look for gold
Convicts were needed to fight in World War I
British jails could not hold the large number of prisoners
questions.explanation: British laws were harsh and the jails could not hold the large number of people imprisoned, so the British Government transported convicts to New South Wales.
questions.source: Part 1 › Early days of European settlement › p. 8

questions.question: To which new colony were the first convicts transported?
questions.explanation: The British Government decided to transport convicts to the new colony of New South Wales.
questions.source: Part 1 › Early days of European settlement › p. 8

questions.question: Captain Arthur Phillip was the first ___ of the colony of New South Wales.
questions.explanation: The first Governor of the colony of New South Wales was Captain Arthur Phillip.
questions.source: Part 1 › Early days of European settlement › p. 8

questions.question: Where did early free settlers come from?
questions.explanation: Early free settlers came from Great Britain and Ireland.
questions.source: Part 1 › Early days of European settlement › p. 8

questions.question: Which heritage has had a major influence on Australia’s recent history, culture and politics?
questions.explanation: Early free settlers came from Great Britain and Ireland, and this British and Irish heritage has had a major influence on Australia’s recent history, culture and politics.
questions.source: Part 1 › Early days of European settlement › p. 8

questions.question: In what year did a ‘gold rush’ begin in Australia?
questions.explanation: In 1851, a ‘gold rush’ began when gold was discovered in the colonies of New South Wales and Victoria.
questions.source: Part 1 › Early days of European settlement › p. 8

questions.question: In which colonies was gold discovered in 1851?
questions.explanation: In 1851, a gold rush began when gold was discovered in the colonies of New South Wales and Victoria.
questions.source: Part 1 › Early days of European settlement › p. 8

questions.question: Who were the first large group of migrants to Australia not from Europe?
options: Chinese people who came during the gold rush
Vietnamese people who came after World War II
People from Türkiye who came after World War I
questions.explanation: Chinese people arriving during the gold rush were the first large group of migrants not from Europe.
questions.source: Part 1 › Early days of European settlement › p. 8

questions.question: What happened to Australia’s population in the 10 years after the gold rush began?
questions.explanation: People from all around the world came to try to make their fortunes. In 10 years, Australia’s population more than doubled.
questions.source: Part 1 › Early days of European settlement › p. 8

questions.question: In 1901, the separate colonies were united into a federation of states called:
options: The Colony of New South Wales
questions.explanation: In 1901, the separate colonies were united into a federation of states called the Commonwealth of Australia.
questions.source: Part 1 › The nation of Australia › p. 9

questions.question: In what year were the separate colonies united into a federation?
questions.explanation: In 1901, the separate colonies were united into a federation of states called the Commonwealth of Australia.
questions.source: Part 1 › The nation of Australia › p. 9

questions.question: Which institutions were established under the new Australian Constitution in 1901?
options: The first convict colony and its first Governor
The Australian Aboriginal Flag and the Torres Strait Islander Flag
The national parliament, government and the High Court
questions.explanation: In 1901, national democratic institutions, including the national parliament, government and the High Court, were established under the new Australian Constitution.
questions.source: Part 1 › The nation of Australia › p. 9

questions.question: What was Australia’s population in 1901, according to the booklet?
questions.explanation: In 1901, Australia’s population was about four million. This number did not include Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
questions.source: Part 1 › The nation of Australia › p. 9

questions.question: After which event were Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples included in official estimates of the Australian population?
options: The end of World War II
questions.explanation: It was not until after a Referendum in 1967 that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples were included in official estimates of the Australian population.
questions.source: Part 1 › The nation of Australia › p. 9

questions.question: What is Australia’s national language?
options: Each state chooses its own national language
Australia does not have a national language
questions.explanation: Australia’s national language is English. It is part of our national identity.
questions.source: Part 1 › The nation of Australia › p. 9

questions.question: In keeping with Australian values, why should migrants learn and use English?
options: To help them participate in Australian society
Because speaking other languages is not allowed
Because English is only needed to vote
questions.explanation: In keeping with Australian values, migrants should learn and use English to help them participate in Australian society. Other languages are also valued.
questions.source: Part 1 › The nation of Australia › p. 9

questions.question: About how many distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages are there?
questions.explanation: Other languages are also valued, including more than 100 distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages.
questions.source: Part 1 › The nation of Australia › p. 9

questions.question: In the first half of the 20th century, there were programs to actively encourage migrants from which country to settle in Australia?
questions.explanation: Throughout the first half of the 20th century, there were programs to actively encourage British migrants to settle in Australia, and many did.
questions.source: Part 1 › The nation of Australia › p. 9

questions.question: When did a wave of non-British migration come to Australia, as millions of people in Europe had to leave their homelands?
questions.explanation: A wave of non-British migration came after World War II, when millions of people in Europe had to leave their homelands.
questions.source: Part 1 › The nation of Australia › p. 9

questions.question: After World War II, large numbers of people came to Australia from which part of the world to build a new life?
questions.explanation: After World War II, large numbers of Europeans came to Australia to build a new life.
questions.source: Part 1 › The nation of Australia › p. 9

questions.question: According to the booklet, why have people come to Australia in recent years?
options: To work as convicts in the colony of New South Wales
To join family, make a new life, or escape poverty, war or persecution
Only to serve in the Australian Defence Force
questions.explanation: In recent years, people have come to Australia to join family, to make a new life, or to escape poverty, war or persecution.
questions.source: Part 1 › The nation of Australia › p. 9

questions.question: While we celebrate the diversity of Australia’s people, what do we also aim to build?
options: Separate communities that do not mix
A nation with one official religion
questions.explanation: While we celebrate the diversity of Australia’s people, we also aim to build a cohesive and unified nation.
questions.source: Part 1 › The nation of Australia › p. 9

questions.question: According to the booklet, why is communicating in English important?
options: It is not important, because other languages are also valued
It is important for making the most of living and working in Australia
It is only important for people who want to vote
questions.explanation: Communicating in English is important for making the most of living and working in Australia.
questions.source: Part 1 › The nation of Australia › p. 9

questions.question: Which statement about languages in Australia is correct?
options: English is the national language, and other languages are also valued
English is the national language, and no other languages are valued
Australia has two national languages: English and one Aboriginal language
questions.explanation: English is the national language, but other languages are also valued, including more than 100 distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages.
questions.source: Part 1 › The nation of Australia › p. 9

questions.question: How many states are there in Australia?
questions.explanation: There are six states and two mainland territories.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 10

questions.question: How many mainland territories are there in Australia?
questions.explanation: There are six states and two mainland territories.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 10

questions.question: What is Australia’s capital city?
questions.explanation: Canberra is Australia’s capital city.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 10

questions.question: What is the capital city of New South Wales?
questions.explanation: Sydney is the capital city of New South Wales.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 10

questions.question: What is the capital city of Victoria?
questions.explanation: Melbourne is the capital city of Victoria.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 10

questions.question: What is the capital city of Queensland?
questions.explanation: Brisbane is the capital city of Queensland.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 10

questions.question: What is the capital city of Western Australia?
questions.explanation: Perth is the capital city of Western Australia.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 10

questions.question: What is the capital city of South Australia?
questions.explanation: Adelaide is the capital city of South Australia.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 10

questions.question: What is the capital city of Tasmania?
questions.explanation: Hobart is the capital city of Tasmania.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 10

questions.question: What is the capital city of the Northern Territory?
questions.explanation: Darwin is the capital city of the Northern Territory.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 10

questions.question: In which state or territory is Canberra?
questions.explanation: The Australian Capital Territory is home to the nation’s capital city, Canberra.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: Which is the largest state in Australia?
questions.explanation: Western Australia is the largest state. Queensland is the second largest.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: Which is the second largest state in Australia?
questions.explanation: Queensland is the second largest state. Western Australia is the largest.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: Which is the smallest state in Australia?
questions.explanation: Tasmania is the smallest state. Victoria is the smallest of the mainland states.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: Which is the smallest of the mainland states?
questions.explanation: Victoria is the smallest of the mainland states. Tasmania is smaller, but it is not on the mainland.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: Which is the nation’s largest city?
questions.explanation: Sydney is the capital city of New South Wales and is the nation’s largest city.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: Which was the first colony established by the British?
questions.explanation: New South Wales was the first colony established by the British.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: Which state is separated from the mainland by the Bass Strait?
questions.explanation: Tasmania is the smallest state, separated from the mainland by the Bass Strait.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: The Great Barrier Reef runs along the eastern coast of which state?
questions.explanation: The world-famous Great Barrier Reef runs along Queensland’s eastern coast.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: Uluru, Kata Tjuta and Kings Canyon are icons of which state or territory?
questions.explanation: Northern Territory icons include Uluru, Kata Tjuta and Kings Canyon.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: Where is the Australian Capital Territory located?
questions.explanation: The Australian Capital Territory is located between Sydney and Melbourne.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: In which city are Parliament House and the High Court of Australia located?
questions.explanation: Several national institutions are located in Canberra, including Parliament House and the High Court of Australia.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: The Sydney Harbour Bridge and Opera House are national icons found in which state?
questions.explanation: Sydney is the capital city of New South Wales. The Sydney Harbour Bridge and Opera House are national icons.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: The Melbourne Cricket Ground, the 12 Apostles and the Royal Exhibition Building are icons of which state?
questions.explanation: Victoria’s icons include the Melbourne Cricket Ground, the 12 Apostles, and the Royal Exhibition Building.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: The Barossa Valley and the Flinders Ranges are icons of which state?
questions.explanation: South Australia’s icons include the Barossa Valley and the Flinders Ranges.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: Cradle Mountain, Port Arthur and the Bay of Fires are icons of which state?
questions.explanation: Tasmanian icons include Cradle Mountain, Port Arthur, and the Bay of Fires.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: The Ningaloo Coast, Margaret River and the Kimberley region are icons of which state?
questions.explanation: Western Australia’s icons include the Ningaloo Coast, Margaret River, and the Kimberley region.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: The Torres Strait Islands lie to the north of which state?
questions.explanation: The Torres Strait Islands lie to the north of Queensland.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s states and territories › p. 11

questions.question: In the booklet, what is an ‘icon’?
questions.explanation: The glossary defines an icon as a well-known image. For example, the booklet calls the Sydney Harbour Bridge and Opera House national icons.
questions.source: Glossary › icon › p. 42

questions.question: Who performs a Welcome to Country?
options: Anyone at the meeting or event who is asked to do it
The Prime Minister or a government minister
An Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian of the local region
questions.explanation: A Welcome to Country is performed by an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian of the local region. Anyone can deliver an Acknowledgement of Country.
questions.source: Part 1 › Traditions › p. 12

questions.question: Who can deliver an Acknowledgement of Country?
options: Only an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian
questions.explanation: Anyone can deliver an Acknowledgement of Country. A Welcome to Country is performed by an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian.
questions.source: Part 1 › Traditions › p. 12

questions.question: At meetings and events, who would generally deliver the Acknowledgement of Country?
options: The Chair or Master of Ceremonies
questions.explanation: At meetings and events, the Acknowledgement of Country would generally be done by the Chair or Master of Ceremonies.
questions.source: Part 1 › Traditions › p. 12

questions.question: When is a Welcome to Country usually held at an event?
options: As the last item, to close the event
As the first item, to open the event
Halfway through, after the main speeches
questions.explanation: A Welcome to Country is usually the first item of proceedings to open an event.
questions.source: Part 1 › Traditions › p. 12

questions.question: Which of these can be part of a Welcome to Country?
questions.explanation: A Welcome to Country can take place through many forms, including songs, dances, smoking ceremonies or speeches in traditional language or English.
questions.source: Part 1 › Traditions › p. 12

questions.question: Why was a Welcome to Country traditionally performed?
options: To collect payment from visitors before they entered the land
To choose a leader for the visitors while they were on that land
To ensure visitors had a safe and protected journey on that land
questions.explanation: A Welcome to Country was traditionally performed to ensure visitors had a safe and protected journey during their time on that land.
questions.source: Part 1 › Traditions › p. 12

questions.question: An Acknowledgement of Country is an opportunity to recognise that the gathering is:
options: On land owned by the Australian Government
On Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander land
questions.explanation: An Acknowledgement of Country is an opportunity to recognise that the gathering is on Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander land.
questions.source: Part 1 › Traditions › p. 12

questions.question: In an Acknowledgement of Country, respect is paid to Traditional Custodians, particularly:
options: The first Governor, Captain Arthur Phillip
questions.explanation: An Acknowledgement of Country pays respect to Traditional Custodians, particularly Elders past and present.
questions.source: Part 1 › Traditions › p. 12

questions.question: Why are Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country practices performed?
options: To show respect for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
To ask the government for permission to hold the event
To celebrate the arrival of the First Fleet
questions.explanation: These practices are performed to show respect for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
questions.source: Part 1 › Traditions › p. 12

questions.question: On what date do we celebrate Australia Day each year?
questions.explanation: On 26 January each year, we celebrate Australia Day.
questions.source: Part 1 › Important days for Australians › p. 13

questions.question: Australia Day is the anniversary of what event?
options: The federation of the colonies in 1901
The arrival of the First Fleet from Great Britain in 1788
questions.explanation: Australia Day is the anniversary of the arrival of the First Fleet from Great Britain in 1788.
questions.source: Part 1 › Important days for Australians › p. 13

questions.question: On what date is Anzac Day commemorated each year?
questions.explanation: Anzac Day is commemorated on 25 April each year.
questions.source: Part 1 › Important days for Australians › p. 13

questions.question: Anzac Day is named after the:
options: Australian and New Zealand Army Corps
Australian and New Zealand Navy Council
questions.explanation: Anzac Day is named after the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps.
questions.source: Part 1 › Important days for Australians › p. 13

questions.question: Where did the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps land on 25 April 1915?
options: Sydney Cove in New South Wales
questions.explanation: The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps landed at Gallipoli in Türkiye during World War I on 25 April 1915.
questions.source: Part 1 › Important days for Australians › p. 13

questions.question: During which war did the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps land at Gallipoli?
options: A war between the colonies before Federation
questions.explanation: The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps landed at Gallipoli in Türkiye during World War I on 25 April 1915.
questions.source: Part 1 › Important days for Australians › p. 13

questions.question: Anzac Day is a solemn day when we remember:
options: The arrival of the First Fleet and the start of European settlement in 1788
The day the separate colonies united to become the Commonwealth of Australia
The sacrifice of all Australians who served and died in wars, conflicts and peacekeeping operations
questions.explanation: Anzac Day is a solemn day when we remember the sacrifice of all Australians who served and died in wars, conflicts and peacekeeping operations.
questions.source: Part 1 › Important days for Australians › p. 13

questions.question: What is the biggest annual public holiday in Australia?
questions.explanation: The booklet says Australia Day is the biggest annual public holiday in Australia.
questions.source: Part 1 › Important days for Australians › p. 13

questions.question: Who announces the Australian of the Year Awards during Australia Day celebrations?
questions.explanation: During Australia Day celebrations, the Prime Minister announces the Australian of the Year Awards in Canberra.
questions.source: Part 1 › Important days for Australians › p. 13

questions.question: In which city are the Australian of the Year Awards announced?
questions.explanation: During Australia Day celebrations, the Prime Minister announces the Australian of the Year Awards in Canberra.
questions.source: Part 1 › Important days for Australians › p. 13

questions.question: Australia Day is marked by events across Australia, including:
questions.explanation: Australia Day is marked by events across Australia, including special citizenship ceremonies.
questions.source: Part 1 › Important days for Australians › p. 13

questions.question: Where is Australia Day a public holiday?
options: In the six states, but not in the territories
In the two mainland territories, but not in the states
questions.explanation: Australia Day is a public holiday in every state and territory in Australia.
questions.source: Part 1 › Important days for Australians › p. 13

questions.question: Which is the official flag of our nation?
questions.explanation: The Australian National Flag is the official flag of our nation. The Australian Aboriginal Flag and the Torres Strait Islander Flag are also officially recognised.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: What colours are the Australian National Flag?
questions.explanation: The Australian National Flag is blue, white and red.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: What is in the top left corner of the Australian National Flag?
questions.explanation: The Union Jack, the flag of the United Kingdom, is in the top left corner.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: What does the Union Jack on the Australian National Flag represent?
options: Our history of British settlement and the laws and institutions we inherited
The six states and the territories that make up the Commonwealth of Australia
A group of stars that can be seen in the southern sky over Australia
questions.explanation: The Union Jack represents our history of British settlement and the laws and institutions we inherited as a result.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: How many points does the Commonwealth Star have?
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth Star has seven points: one for each of the six states and one for the territories.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: What do the points of the Commonwealth Star represent?
options: Seven states, one point for each
The six states, plus one point for the territories
questions.explanation: Each point represents one of the six states, and one point is for the territories.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: Where is the Commonwealth Star on the Australian National Flag?
options: In the centre of the flag
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth Star is under the Union Jack.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: What is the Southern Cross on the Australian National Flag?
options: The flag of the United Kingdom, in the top left corner
A symbol for the six states and federation
A group of stars that can be seen in the southern sky
questions.explanation: The Southern Cross, on the right of the flag, is a group of stars that can be seen in the southern sky.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: What colours are the Australian Aboriginal Flag?
questions.explanation: The Australian Aboriginal Flag is black, red and yellow.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: On the Australian Aboriginal Flag, what does the black top half represent?
questions.explanation: The top half of the Aboriginal Flag is black and represents the Aboriginal peoples of Australia.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: On the Australian Aboriginal Flag, what does the red bottom half represent?
questions.explanation: The bottom half is red and represents the earth, which has ceremonial significance.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: On the Australian Aboriginal Flag, what does the yellow circle represent?
questions.explanation: The yellow circle on the Australian Aboriginal Flag represents the sun.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: What colours are the Torres Strait Islander Flag?
questions.explanation: The Torres Strait Islander Flag is green, blue, black and white.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: On the Torres Strait Islander Flag, what do the green stripes represent?
questions.explanation: The green stripes on the Torres Strait Islander Flag represent the land.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: On the Torres Strait Islander Flag, what does the blue panel in the centre represent?
questions.explanation: The blue panel in the centre represents the sea.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: On the Torres Strait Islander Flag, what is the white dancer’s headdress a symbol for?
options: The six states and the territories
questions.explanation: The white dancer’s headdress in the centre is a symbol for all Torres Strait Islanders.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: On the Torres Strait Islander Flag, what do the points of the white star represent?
options: The six states and the territories
The island groups in the Torres Strait
The stars of the Southern Cross
questions.explanation: The points of the white star represent the island groups in the Torres Strait.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: On the Torres Strait Islander Flag, what does the colour white symbolise?
questions.explanation: The colour white on the Torres Strait Islander Flag symbolises peace.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s flags › p. 14

questions.question: Which two animals support the shield on the Commonwealth Coat of Arms?
questions.explanation: A kangaroo and an emu support the shield on each side. Both are native Australian animals.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s symbols › p. 15

questions.question: What does the shield in the centre of the Commonwealth Coat of Arms represent?
questions.explanation: The shield in the centre of the Coat of Arms represents the six states and federation.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s symbols › p. 15

questions.question: What sits above the shield on the Commonwealth Coat of Arms?
questions.explanation: A gold Commonwealth Star sits above the shield.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s symbols › p. 15

questions.question: What is in the background of the Commonwealth Coat of Arms?
questions.explanation: The background of the Coat of Arms is the golden wattle, Australia’s national flower.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s symbols › p. 15

questions.question: What is the official symbol of the Commonwealth of Australia?
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth Coat of Arms is the official symbol of the Commonwealth of Australia. The golden wattle is the national flower and the opal is the national gemstone.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s symbols › p. 15

questions.question: What does the Commonwealth Coat of Arms identify?
options: The authority and property of the Commonwealth of Australia
The capital city of each state and territory
The uniforms of Australia’s national sports teams
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth Coat of Arms represents our national unity and identifies the authority and property of the Commonwealth of Australia.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s symbols › p. 15

questions.question: What is Australia’s national flower?
questions.explanation: Australia’s national flower is the golden wattle.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s symbols › p. 15

questions.question: Where does the golden wattle mainly grow?
options: In the tropical rainforests of Queensland
In the dry red desert of the Northern Territory
questions.explanation: The golden wattle is a small tree that grows mainly in south-eastern Australia.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s symbols › p. 15

questions.question: In which season does the golden wattle have many golden yellow flowers?
questions.explanation: The golden wattle has bright green leaves and many golden yellow flowers in spring.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s symbols › p. 15

questions.question: What are Australia’s national colours?
questions.explanation: Australia’s national colours are green and gold, the colours of the golden wattle.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s symbols › p. 15

questions.question: Australia’s national colours of green and gold come from:
questions.explanation: Australia’s national colours are green and gold, the colours of the golden wattle.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s symbols › p. 15

questions.question: What is Australia’s national gemstone?
questions.explanation: The opal is Australia’s national gemstone.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s symbols › p. 15

questions.question: According to Aboriginal legend, how were the colours of the opal created?
options: A star fell into the desert
questions.explanation: According to Aboriginal legend, a rainbow touched the earth and created the colours of the opal.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s symbols › p. 15

questions.question: Which statement about floral emblems is correct?
options: Each state and territory also has its own floral emblem
The golden wattle is the floral emblem of every state and territory
The six states have floral emblems, but the territories do not
questions.explanation: Each of the states and territories of Australia also has its own floral emblem.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s symbols › p. 15

questions.question: In the booklet, what is a ‘floral emblem’?
questions.explanation: The glossary defines a floral emblem as a national flower. Australia’s national flower is the golden wattle.
questions.source: Glossary › floral emblem › p. 41

questions.question: What is Australia’s national anthem?
questions.explanation: ‘Advance Australia Fair’ is Australia’s national anthem. The other options are lines from it.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s national anthem › p. 16

questions.question: When is the national anthem sung?
options: On occasions of national importance, such as citizenship ceremonies and major sporting events
Only on Anzac Day, as part of the solemn ceremony at dawn
Only when parliament opens after a federal election
questions.explanation: ‘Advance Australia Fair’ is sung on occasions of national importance, including at Australian citizenship ceremonies and major sporting events.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s national anthem › p. 16

questions.question: Which line opens Australia’s national anthem?
options: With courage let us all combine
questions.explanation: The anthem opens with ‘Australians all let us rejoice, For we are one and free’.
questions.source: Part 1 › Australia’s national anthem › p. 16

questions.question: In the booklet, what is a ‘national anthem’?
questions.explanation: The glossary defines a national anthem as a national song. Australia’s national anthem is ‘Advance Australia Fair’.
questions.source: Glossary › national anthem › p. 42

questions.question: According to the booklet, Australian values are based on which ideas?
options: Wealth, social class, gender and ethnicity
Religious law, family status and personal wealth
Freedom, respect, fairness and equality of opportunity
questions.explanation: Australian values are based on freedom, respect, fairness and equality of opportunity.
questions.source: Part 4 › Australian values › p. 34

questions.topic: Commitment to the Rule of Law
questions.question: According to the booklet, what happens if you break the law in Australia?
options: Nothing, if you did not know the law
Only a warning, the first time
questions.explanation: Everybody should obey the law and not break it at any time, otherwise they will face penalties. Not knowing the law is no excuse.
questions.source: Part 4 › Commitment to the Rule of Law › p. 34

questions.question: Why does the power of the government come from the Australian people?
options: Citizens vote for their representatives in parliament
Citizens elect the judges and magistrates of every court
Citizens elect the Governor-General at every election
questions.explanation: The power of the government comes from the Australian people because Australian citizens vote for people to represent them in parliament.
questions.source: Part 4 › Parliamentary democracy › p. 34

questions.question: Is it legal in Australia to make false allegations about another person?
options: Yes, if it is only said in private
questions.explanation: Freedom of speech has limits. It is illegal to make false allegations.
questions.source: Part 4 › Freedom of speech › p. 35

questions.question: What freedom do newspapers, television and radio outlets have in Australia?
options: Only the freedom to report the government’s views
No freedom, unless the government approves
The same freedom of speech as people
questions.explanation: People are free to say and write what they think. Newspapers, television and radio outlets have the same freedom.
questions.source: Part 4 › Freedom of speech › p. 35

questions.question: A member of a social club decides to leave it. What does the booklet say?
options: Members need the leaders’ permission to leave
People are free to leave any group voluntarily
Members can be forced to stay once they join
questions.explanation: In Australia, people are free to join or leave any group voluntarily, as long as it is within the law.
questions.source: Part 4 › Freedom of association › p. 35

questions.question: What can happen to someone who forces another person into a marriage in Australia?
options: Only a warning, if the families agree
Nothing, if religious law allows it
questions.explanation: Forced marriage is against the law in Australia and can result in severe legal penalties, including imprisonment.
questions.source: Part 4 › Freedom of religion › p. 35

questions.question: What legal status do religious laws have in Australia?
options: The same status as Australian law
A higher status than Australian law
questions.explanation: Religious laws have no legal status in Australia. Australian law must be followed by everyone.
questions.source: Part 4 › Freedom of religion › p. 35

questions.topic: Equality of all people under the law
questions.question: A woman wants to join the Australian Defence Force. What does the booklet say?
options: Only men can join the Defence Force
Men and women have equal access to join it
Women can join only if a husband agrees
questions.explanation: Men and women have equal rights. Both can join the Australian Defence Force and the police force.
questions.source: Part 4 › Equality of all people under the law › p. 36

questions.topic: Equality of all people under the law
questions.question: A wife wants a divorce, but her husband wants to stay married. Can she apply for a divorce?
options: No, both spouses must agree to a divorce
Yes, either spouse may apply to the courts
Only if her religious leader approves
questions.explanation: Divorce is acceptable in Australia. Either a husband or a wife may apply to the courts for a divorce, even if the other spouse wishes to continue the marriage.
questions.source: Part 4 › Equality of all people under the law › p. 36

questions.topic: Equality of opportunity and a ‘fair go’
questions.question: Your cousin says people from wealthy families deserve the best jobs. Which Australian value does this go against?
options: Equality of opportunity and a ‘fair go’
questions.explanation: Everyone deserves a ‘fair go’. A person should get a job based on their skills and experience, not because of their wealth.
questions.source: Part 4 › Equality of opportunity and a ‘fair go’ › p. 36

questions.topic: Mutual respect and tolerance for others
questions.question: During an argument, one neighbour shouts insults and threats at another. What does the booklet say?
options: Only physical violence is against the law
Shouting threats is fine if no one is hurt
Verbal abuse is illegal, like physical abuse
questions.explanation: It is against the law to be violent towards another person. Violence of any kind, including verbal and physical abuse, is illegal.
questions.source: Part 4 › Mutual respect and tolerance for others › p. 37

questions.topic: Mutual respect and tolerance for others
questions.question: Why should you obey a lawful request from the police?
options: The police make the laws in Australia
The police decide who is guilty in court
All Australians commit to following the law
questions.explanation: You should obey a lawful request from the police, because all Australians commit to following the law. Parliament makes the laws, and courts decide if a person is guilty.
questions.source: Part 4 › Mutual respect and tolerance for others › p. 37

questions.question: According to the booklet, what does everyone have a responsibility to do when they are able?
options: Rely on other people to support them
Leave supporting families to the government
Try to support themselves and their families
questions.explanation: Everyone has a responsibility to try and support themselves and their families when they are able to do so.
questions.source: Part 4 › Making a contribution › p. 38

questions.question: In the booklet, what does ‘mateship’ mean?
options: Joining a trade union with your friends
Helping only people from your own culture
Helping others, and receiving help, in hard times
questions.explanation: Mateship means helping and receiving help from others, especially in difficult times.
questions.source: Glossary › mateship › p. 42

questions.question: If English is not their native language, what must applicants for Australian citizenship undertake to do?
options: Make reasonable efforts to learn English
Stop using their first language at home
Speak only English with their children
questions.explanation: Applicants for Australian citizenship must undertake to make reasonable efforts to learn the English language, if it is not their native language.
questions.source: Part 4 › English as the national language › p. 38

questions.topic: Helping to keep our society safe
questions.question: You suspect your neighbour may be planning to commit a serious crime. What should you do?
options: Report it to government authorities quickly
Say nothing, as it is a private matter
Wait until the crime has happened first
questions.explanation: If people suspect a friend or neighbour may be planning to commit a serious crime, they should report this to Australian government authorities as soon as possible.
questions.source: Part 4 › Helping to keep our society safe › p. 38

questions.question: Can an Australian citizen also be a citizen of another country?
options: Yes, if that country’s laws allow it
Only if they live outside Australia
questions.explanation: Australian citizens may also hold the citizenship of another country or countries if the laws of those countries allow. This is known as dual, or multiple, citizenship.
questions.source: Part 4 › Loyalty to Australia › p. 38

questions.question: Someone uses social media to share official government secrets. What does the booklet say?
options: It is protected by freedom of speech
It is fine if the secrets are old
questions.explanation: Australian society is based on shared obligations not to undermine Australia’s interests and security. Using social media to share official government secrets would undermine Australia’s interests.
questions.source: Part 4 › Loyalty to Australia › p. 38

questions.question: According to the booklet, what has created Australia’s peaceful and stable society?
options: One official religion and one set of beliefs
A single political party that runs the country
questions.explanation: Our democratic institutions and shared Australian values have created our peaceful and stable society.
questions.source: Part 4 › In conclusion › p. 39
